titleStmt.title: Processing of natural images is feedforward: a simple behavioral test
titleStmt.author: Schmidt
Schmidt

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Processing of natural images is feedforward: a simple behavioral test

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our data indicate that prime and target signals remained strictly sequential throughout all processing stages, meeting unprecedentedly stringent behavioral criteria for feedforward processing (rapid-chase criteria).

span.label: visuomotor response priming with natural images
span.quote: We tested this theory in a visuomotor priming task in which speeded pointing responses were performed toward one of two target images containing a prespecified stimulus (e.g., animal vs. nonanimal, ellipse vs. rectangle).

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: We compared four tasks in two experiments to demonstrate rapid-chase processing of natural images.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The prime's feedforward wave arrives at motor areas first and drives the movement alone until the target's wave arrives and takes over; a longer SOA gives the prime a longer unopposed drive, which is why priming grows with SOA.
span.quote: Priming effects increase with prime–target SOA because the prime has more time to drive the response on its own when the target is further delayed.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: When no overt detour appears, opposing prime- and target-driven response tendencies conflict covertly and must be resolved before the movement can start, which shows up as a delayed onset instead.
span.quote: Even in the absence of detours, the delay of pointing onset probably reflects a covert conflict of opposing response tendencies from prime and target signals that must be resolved before movement onset can occur

span.label: The paper does not claim that the rapid classification is driven by image semantics specifically.
span.quote: However, we make no claim here that classification is based exclusively on the semantic content of the images.

span.label: In the slow large-small task the independence criterion could not be clearly evaluated.
span.quote: Only in the large–small task, with its tardy response dynamics and small priming effects, does it become difficult to evaluate whether the independence criterion is met.

span.label: In Experiment 1 the raw trajectories did not show the initiation criterion; the conclusion rests on the derived spatial priming functions.
span.quote: Admittedly, these issues are less clear in Experiment 1, in which both tasks failed to meet the initiation criterion, at least when judged by looking only at the raw trajectories (Figure 2).

span.label: Meeting the rapid-chase criteria shows behavioural equivalence to a feedforward system, not that every processing substage is feedforward.
span.quote: Importantly, note that the rapid-chase criteria do not guarantee that a stimulus– response system is strictly feedforward in all its substages (and they actually do not require such a strict assumption), but they reveal whether a system is behaviorally equivalent to a simple feedforward system.

span.label: rapid-chase criteria
span.quote: The feedforward properties of the system would show in the time course of the response and meet the following rapid-chase criteria

span.label: feedforward
span.quote: In the context of neuronal signal flow, feedforward indicates that a cell passes activation on to another cell before integrating any feedback or recurrent information from other cells about that signal

span.label: independence criterion
span.quote: response kinematics should initially depend exclusively on prime characteristics and be independent of all target characteristics (independence criterion). The initiation criterion guarantees that the prime wins the chase

span.label: priming effects
span.quote: Priming effects increase with prime–target SOA because the prime has more time to drive the response on its own when the target is further delayed

span.label: **THREE NAMED CRITERIA, EACH WITH ITS JOB STATED - THE CLEAREST `a tool must be checkable` IN THIS CORPUS:** `(1) Prime rather than target signals should determine the onset and initial direction of the response (INITIATION CRITERION); (2) target signals should be able to influence the response before it is completed (TAKEOVER CRITERION); and, crucially, (3) response kinematics should initially depend exclusively on prime characteristics and be independent of all target characteristics (INDEPENDENCE CRITERION).` **Numbered, named, and separately falsifiable** - a dataset can meet 1 and 2 and fail 3, which is exactly what happens in one of this paper's four tasks. Compare jitendra2016, which grades a literature against someone else's published checklist: same discipline, applied to a mechanism instead of a field
span.quote: 1) Prime rather than target signals should determine the onset and initial direction of the response (initiation criterion); (2) target signals should be able to influence the response before it is completed (takeover criterion); and, crucially, (3) response kinematics should initially depend exclusively on prime characteristics and be independent of all target characteristics (independence criterion). The initiation criterion guarantees that the prime wins the chase

span.label: **AND THE CLAIM IS EQUIVALENCE, NOT IDENTITY, STATED BY THE AUTHORS IN THEIR OWN CONCLUSION:** `our data indicate a rapid-chase system ... that is BEHAVIORALLY EQUIVALENT to a feedforward system with high temporal resolution.` They say elsewhere that the criteria `do not guarantee that a stimulus-response system is strictly feedforward in all its substages`. **A behavioural test that names the limit of what behaviour can establish.** Most records in this corpus infer a mechanism from a behavioural measure; this one declines to, and says which claim the method does support instead
span.quote: our data indicate a rapid-chase system (Schmidt et al., 2006; Vath & Schmidt, 2007) that is behaviorally equivalent to a feedforward system with high temporal resolution

span.label: **THE PAPER CONTAINS ITS OWN BOUNDARY CONDITION - ONE OF FOUR TASKS FAILS:** `Only in the LARGE-SMALL TASK, with its tardy response dynamics and small priming effects, does it become difficult to evaluate whether the INDEPENDENCE CRITERION is met.` And the diagnosis is offered rather than withheld: `it rather seems that the large-small classification CANNOT BE PERFORMED IN A SINGLE FEEDFORWARD SWEEP and requires more extensive, RECURRENT processing.` **Same images, same participants, same apparatus - only the classification rule changed, and the account stops applying.** A scope limit measured inside the paper rather than conceded to a critic later
span.quote: Only in the large–small task, with its tardy response dynamics and small priming effects, does it become difficult to evaluate whether the independence criterion is met

span.label: **AND THE DOSE-RESPONSE COMES WITH ITS MECHANISM ATTACHED, WHICH IS RARE:** `Priming effects increase with prime-target SOA BECAUSE THE PRIME HAS MORE TIME TO DRIVE THE RESPONSE ON ITS OWN when the target is further delayed.` The `because` is not decoration - it is the rapid-chase model making the prediction, and the effect size is a duration rather than a strength. **dijksterhuis1998 doses by prime DURATION and gets a bigger effect; this doses by the GAP and gets a longer unopposed run** - two different quantities that both look like `more priming` in a results table
span.quote: Priming effects increase with prime–target SOA because the prime has more time to drive the response on its own when the target is further delayed

span.label: extends → the authors' own rapid-chase theory of response priming (Schmidt et al., 2006; Vath & Schmidt, 2007)
span.quote: Our results extend our rapid-chase theory of response priming to the domain of natural image processing, linking visuomotor priming to feedforward processing of images (Schmidt et al., 2006; Vath & Schmidt, 2007).

span.label: builds-on → rapid natural-scene categorisation studies (Bacon-Macé et al., 2007; Kirchner & Thorpe, 2006; Thorpe et al., 1996; VanRullen & Koch, 2003; VanRullen & Thorpe, 2001, 2002)
span.quote: Our data strongly support the conclusion from previous studies (e.g., Bacon-Macé et al., 2007; Kirchner & Thorpe, 2006; Thorpe et al., 1996; VanRullen & Koch, 2003; Van- Rullen & Thorpe, 2001, 2002) that natural scenes can be classified on the basis of an initial feedforward sweep of processing (Bullier, 2001; Lamme & Roelfsema, 2000).

span.label: contradicts → the claim that natural image classification is "ultra-rapid" (Kirchner & Thorpe, 2006; VanRullen & Thorpe, 2001)
span.quote: These differences considered, there is no indication here that natural image classification is extraordinarily fast, or “ultra-rapid” (Kirchner & Thorpe, 2006; VanRullen & Thorpe, 2001), when compared with even more basic tasks such as simple shape classification.

span.label: feedforward —operationalised-as→ rapid-chase criteria
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — **THE WHOLE PAPER IN ONE EDGE, AND `would show in the time course of the response` IS THE OPERATIONALISATION.** A claim about neuronal signal flow is turned into three tests on a pointing trajectory. Weight 0.95: the criteria are named, numbered and separately checkable, and the authors state in the same passage that meeting them establishes BEHAVIOURAL EQUIVALENCE and not strict feedforward - so the edge is exactly as strong as the paper says it is, which is why it earns 0.95 rather than being hedged down.
span.quote: The feedforward properties of the system would show in the time course of the response and meet the following rapid-chase criteria

span.label: independence criterion —part-of→ rapid-chase criteria
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE THIRD OF THREE, and the quote carries all three in order with their names. Recorded separately because it is the one that FAILS in the large-small task - a corpus that holds only `rapid-chase criteria` as one node cannot express that a system met two of them. Weight 0.95: the membership is explicit in the enumeration.
span.quote: The feedforward properties of the system would show in the time course of the response and meet the following rapid-chase criteria: (1) Prime rather than target signals should determine the onset and initial direction of the response (initiation criterion); (2) target signals should be able to influence the response before it is completed (takeover criterion); and, crucially, (3) response kinematics should initially depend exclusively on prime characteristics and be independent of all target characteristics (independence criterion). The initiation criterion guarantees that the prime wins the chase

span.label: F-test / ANOVA
span.quote: Finally, F tests and standard error bars were corrected to estimate variation among participants, rather than among subsamples.

span.label: jackknife
span.quote: Kinematic parameters of trajectories and spatial priming functions were extracted by jackknifing methods (Ulrich & Miller, 2001).

span.label: arcsine transformation
span.quote: Accordingly, analysis of the arcsine-transformed error rates confirmed a main effect of consistency

span.label: data smoothing filter
span.quote: Averaged trajectories in the subsamples were then smoothed with a T4253H filter (Velleman, 1980).

span.label: standard error
span.quote: Error bars are corrected for between-subjects variance (Bakeman & McArthur, 1996).

span.label: In the animal-versus-object task, the time course of spatial priming matched the pattern the rapid-chase model predicts.
span.quote: In the animal–object task, the time course of spatial priming effects (Figure 4A) conformed to the pattern predicted by the rapid-chase model

span.label: Spatial priming curves for every prime-target SOA followed one identical initial trajectory and separated only later, in SOA order, showing the target had no influence on the response when the prime first moved it.
span.quote: Crucially, the early time course of spatial priming was invariant for the different SOAs: All curves initially follow the time course of the curve for the longest SOA, in line with the independence criterion, and branch off only later one by one in the order of increasing SOAs.

span.label: The large-versus-small size-judgement task was the one case where the independence criterion could not be assessed, because its responses were slow and its priming effects small.
span.quote: Only in the large–small task, with its tardy response dynamics and small priming effects, does it become difficult to evaluate whether the independence criterion is met.

span.label: The authors attribute the slowness of the size-judgement task to its needing recurrent processing rather than a single feedforward sweep.
span.quote: It rather seems that the large–small classification cannot be performed in a single feedforward sweep and requires more extensive, recurrent processing.

span.label: Natural-image categorisation was not unusually fast when benchmarked against simple ellipse-versus-rectangle shape classification, undercutting the label 'ultra-rapid'.
span.quote: These differences considered, there is no indication here that natural image classification is extraordinarily fast, or “ultra-rapid”

span.label: When prime and target categories conflicted, the pointing hand physically veered into the quadrant indicated by the prime before reversing toward the correct target.
span.quote: In inconsistent trials, however, the sensor tended to detour into the quadrant specified by the misleading prime before reversing and proceeding in the correct direction.

span.label: Pointing errors occurred almost only on inconsistent trials and grew with prime-target SOA, showing prime influence reaches the motor level.
span.quote: Errors occur mainly in inconsistent trials, and there increase with SOA, further showing that the impact of the primes goes all the way to the level of motor processing

span.label: The authors conclude that visuomotor priming reads out the first pass of information through the visuomotor system, before recurrent processing contributes.
span.quote: Our data thus suggest that visuomotor priming effects can capture the output of the very first pass of information through the visuomotor system, prior to contributions from recurrent processing.

span.label: feedforward (in neuronal signal flow)
span.quote: In the context of neuronal signal flow, feedforward indicates that a cell passes activation on to another cell before integrating any feedback or recurrent information from other cells about that signal.

span.label: rapid chase
span.quote: In a simple feedforward system that is reasonably fast and has sufficient temporal resolution, prime and target signals would engage in what we call a rapid chase, with the prime signal maintaining a lead over the target signal all the way to motor control.

span.label: rapid-chase criteria (initiation, takeover, independence)
span.quote: The feedforward properties of the system would show in the time course of the response and meet the following rapid-chase criteria: (1) Prime rather than target signals should determine the onset and initial direction of the response (initiation criterion); (2) target signals should be able to influence the response before it is completed (takeover criterion); and, crucially, (3) response kinematics should initially depend exclusively on prime characteristics and be independent of all target characteristics (independence criterion).

span.label: independence criterion
span.quote: The initiation criterion guarantees that the prime wins the chase; the takeover criterion guarantees that the chase is sufficiently fast to take place within a single response; and the independence criterion establishes strict sequentiality of response control.

span.label: spatial priming function
span.quote: In addition, we defined a spatial priming function by subtracting trajectories in consistent trails from those in inconsistent trials

span.label: prime-target stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA)
span.quote: After a prime–target SOA of 33, 50, 67, 83, or 100 msec, two target images were presented at the same locations as the primes.

span.label: prime-target consistency
span.quote: In consistent trials, primes and targets from the same category were presented at corresponding positions; in inconsistent trials, prime positions were switched.

span.label: classification task (animal-object, large-small, toy-animal-object, ellipse-rectangle)
span.quote: In each experiment, the participants took part in eight experimental sessions, four in each of the two respective tasks, with task order counterbalanced across participants.

span.label: pointing trajectory position over time
span.quote: Pointing responses were recorded by a Polhemus FASTRAK magnetic tracking device at a sampling frequency of 120 Hz.

span.label: response error rate
span.quote: Lower panels: Rates of response errors, which are defined as arrivals of the sensor at the nontarget position.

span.label: 380 msec — time after prime onset at which the hand began moving on consistent trials in the large-small task (versus roughly 300 msec in the animal-object task)
span.quote: animal–object task (Figure 2A) and roughly 380 msec after prime onset in the large–small task (Figure 2B).

span.label: 280 msec / 220 msec — movement onset times after prime onset in the toy-animal-object and ellipse-rectangle tasks of Experiment 2
span.quote: Indeed, movements started earlier, roughly 280 msec after prime onset in the toy-animal–object task and roughly 220 msec after prime onset in the ellipse–rectangle task

span.label: 160 msec — lag of priming-effect onset in the large-small task relative to the ellipse-rectangle task
span.quote: those in the large– small task developed a full 160 msec after those in the ellipse– rectangle task.

span.label: 33, 50, 67, 83, or 100 msec — the five prime-target stimulus onset asynchronies used, with primes shown for 33 msec
span.quote: The primes appeared for 33 msec at prime–target stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs) of 33, 50, 67, 83, or 100 msec.

span.label: Twelve — total participants, six in each of the two experiments
span.quote: Twelve students from the University of Giessen (Experiment 1, 6 participants, 20–29 years of age, 1 male, 1 left-handed; Experiment 2, 6 participants, 21–30 years of age, 2 male, all right-handed) volunteered for course credit or for a payment of €8/h.

span.label: 1.14% and 1.73% — trials discarded by the exclusion rules in Experiments 1 and 2
span.quote: This procedure eliminated 1.14% and 1.73% of the trials in Experiments 1 and 2, respectively.

span.label: about 80 msec — how much earlier spatial priming onset occurred in the animal-object task than in the large-small task
span.quote: This criterion was crossed about 80 msec earlier in the animal-object task than in the large–small task
